newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU farm ministers try to head off mad cow crisis.
newsitem.headline: EU farm ministers try to head off mad cow crisis.

text.p: European Union Farm Ministers planned intensive informal discussions on Monday to head off a new crisis with Britain over its suspension of a cattle cull agreed under a plan to wipe out mad cow disease.

Britain's EU partners voiced anger at London's failure to kill up to 147,000 young cattle under a plan to get a ban on British beef exports lifted, but said they would use the next 48 hours to ward off a potentially fractious showdown.
"We can talk a lot today and tomorrow have a meeting to summarise and try to find a solution," French Farm Minister Philippe Vasseur told reporters.

The Netherlands' Agriculture Minister, Jozias Van Aartsen, voiced disappointment at the way Britain unilaterally announced last week that it was suspending the extra cull because new evidence showed it would not hasten the end of BSE.
"I don't think it was wise to do it the way the British government did it. But I think we should see what they are going to do in coming months," Aartsen said.
"I don't think there is a crisis yet. But it is a further difficult moment in this whole long journey."
Portugal's Fernando Gomez da Silva said Lisbon was irritated at the way Britain suddenly announced that new scientific evidence had thrown the Florence summit agreement on the cull into doubt.

"I think it was better to discuss a little with the community before taking the decision," he said. Asked what chance he saw of the ban on British beef exports being lifted in current circumstances he replied: "Very, very little."
He and other ministers said they would use the occasion of a three-day informal EU meeting in this southern Irish town to quiz Britain's Douglas Hogg over London's latest moves.
The Killarney talks were supposed to review schemes to restore confidence in beef after Britain said in March there was a link between BSE and a fatal brain-wasting disease in humans.
Hogg, unfazed by media headlines suggesting Britain was again in the dock for its go-it-alone European policies, said the atmosphere at the talks was "very good."
"This is an informal meeting about the long term trends of the beef industry," he told reporters. "We are going to make steady progress over a period of time."

He said he would be pressing his EU partners to go ahead with a package agreed at an EU summit in Florence under which Britain reluctantly agreed to the extra cull in a bid to get the world export ban lifted.
But EU Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler said on Sunday that there would be no lifting of the ban until Britain carried out the EU Florence pact in full.

Hogg said he hoped to press his colleagues to enact the next stage of the plan which would allow the ban to be lifted on so-called certified herds which have been fed on grass rather than protein meal.
The EU Commission and veterinary scientists are currently studying Britain's latest evidence from Oxford academics and are expected to report back in late October.
Hogg found some support from Van Aartsen, who said his government would look sympathtically at the scheme to ease the ban on certified herds.

"I think the point of going towards a more selective way of culling and looking towards the possibility of lifting a ban for BSE-free herds is an idea the Dutch government has advanced for a long time," he said.
